findings.evidence: features/006-insights-skill/006-insights-skill-prd.md:R6 + R7 + AC-6 + AC-7 — R6 specifies cron is user-wired (skill never installs a scheduler) but the cadence knob `config.json.insights.cadence` has four values (`weekly`, `monthly`, `quarterly`, `manual-only`) and R7 specifies a chat-line emission of next-suggested-run date computed from `last_successful_run_at + cadence_interval`. AC-7 names the cadence-interval mapping: `weekly = 7 days, monthly = 30 days, quarterly = 90 days; manual-only emits 'no scheduled cadence — invoke manually'`. But the PRD does NOT articulate the load-bearing assumption underneath the cadence-knob design: the skill's behaviour is identical regardless of which cadence value is set — the cadence knob ONLY affects the chat-line's next-suggested-run-date computation. The skill never refuses, blocks, or behaves differently across cadence values; the user's external scheduler does the actual cadence enforcement. R7 says 'the chat-line is informational only — the skill never blocks on too-soon re-runs (the user's scheduler owns cadence enforcement)' but the load-bearing fact that the cadence knob has zero behavioural effect inside the skill is buried. A future reader (or a downstream consumer integrating with the cadence knob) might infer the skill enforces cadence somehow — it doesn't. The interview's Round 3 resolution has the same buried framing: 'The knob's existence keeps the cadence surface visible in `config.json` for users to tune, and lets the skill compute the next-suggested-run date deterministically.' The PRD captures the chat-line emission (R7) but doesn't name the assumption that the cadence knob is purely informational and has no enforcement semantics inside the skill. Without this articulated, a v2 PRD adding cadence enforcement (e.g. 'refuse runs within X days of the previous run') would silently break the v1 contract because v1 readers would have inferred enforcement from the knob's existence.
findings.claim: Missing tradeoff articulation + unstated load-bearing assumption — R6 + R7 + AC-7 describe the cadence knob's chat-line behaviour but never articulate the load-bearing assumption that the cadence knob is PURELY INFORMATIONAL inside the skill — it changes only the chat-line, never enforces cadence, never blocks runs, never changes cluster-detection behaviour. Think Before Coding principle: 'Don't hide confusion. Surface tradeoffs. State assumptions explicitly.' The assumption is buried in R7's 'informational only' parenthetical but not named as a contract. Downstream consumers (a v2 enhancement adding scheduler installation, an external tool reading `config.json.insights.cadence` to schedule its own jobs) cannot tell from the PRD whether the cadence knob controls anything inside the skill. The corpus loses signal.
findings.proposed_change: Two options: (a) add an explicit requirement R{new} naming the cadence knob's purely-informational status: 'Cadence knob is informational only. The `config.json.insights.cadence` value affects ONLY R7's chat-line next-suggested-run-date computation; the value never causes the skill to refuse, block, or behave differently. Cluster detection runs identically across all cadence values. External schedulers (the user's GH Actions cron, system cron, Linear automation) own cadence enforcement.' AND extend AC-6 to verify: 'On every run, cluster-detection behaviour is identical regardless of `config.json.insights.cadence` value — running with cadence=`weekly` produces the same cluster output as cadence=`manual-only` on the same corpus.' OR (b) extend R6 + R7 with a Note articulating the assumption as a contract: 'Note: the cadence knob is purely informational inside this skill. It changes only R7's chat-line; cluster detection and refusal logic are cadence-independent. v2 enhancements adding cadence enforcement (refuse-too-soon, etc.) would be breaking changes.' Option (a) makes the assumption mechanically observable via AC-6's expanded check; option (b) is documentation-only. Either resolves the unstated assumption.

findings.evidence: features/006-insights-skill/006-insights-skill-prd.md:R9 + AC-9 — R9 specifies the tier-routing logic for promotion proposals: 'clusters where contributing entries cite a pattern that has NO existing guideline ... propose observation→guideline; clusters where contributing entries cite a pattern that DOES have an existing guideline AND surface ≥3 distinct guideline-flagged violations propose guideline→non-negotiable.' AC-9 names the detection signals: 'signalled by the contributing entries' `escaped_issues.descriptions[i]` or `what_didnt_work` substrings naming the existing rule's `id`'. The implicit assumption is that guideline-flagged violations are distinguishable from observation-level patterns by substring-matching the rule `id` in the free-text retro fields. But the alternative — a richer signal where `task-history.json` entries explicitly cite the rule(s) they violated via a structured `rule_violations: ["RULE_ID", ...]` field — is not articulated as a tradeoff. The substring-matching approach has known false-positive risks (e.g. a rule id like `NO_HARDCODED_VALUES` matches any retro field mentioning the phrase, even in unrelated context like 'discussed NO_HARDCODED_VALUES in the design review without applying it') and known false-negative risks (the user describes a violation in prose without ever mentioning the rule id). The structured-field alternative would be a `specflow:complete` schema enhancement (cross-skill change), but the PRD picks substring-matching without naming the cost.
findings.claim: Single-interpretation framing of a tradeoff that has two viable approaches — R9's substring-match-on-rule-id approach for detecting guideline-flagged violations eliminates the alternative of a structured `rule_violations` field on task-history.json entries, without articulating why the elimination happened or what the substring approach's false-positive/false-negative costs are. Think Before Coding principle: 'Present multiple interpretations when ambiguity exists. Push back when a simpler approach exists.' The substring approach was chosen without naming the cost; the structured-field alternative was eliminated silently.
findings.proposed_change: Edit R9 to articulate the tradeoff explicitly: 'R9 detects guideline-flagged violations via substring-match on the rule's id in contributing entries' free-text retro fields (`escaped_issues.descriptions[i]`, `what_didnt_work`). Tradeoff: substring matching is implementation-cheap and works against the existing task-history.json schema, but has known false-positive risks (rule id mentioned in unrelated context) and false-negative risks (user describes violation in prose without naming the rule). Decision: v1 ships substring matching to avoid a cross-skill task-history.json schema change; v2 may add a structured `rule_violations: ["RULE_ID", ...]` field on task-history.json entries (specflow:complete schema enhancement) for higher-fidelity detection. The v1 false-positive risk is mitigated by R8's three-option user prompt — every promotion is human-confirmed, so a substring false-positive surfaces a proposal the user rejects rather than auto-promoting noise. The v1 false-negative risk is the cost of substring-matching's lexical-not-semantic limit; embedding-based matching would address it but is out-of-scope per R3.' This makes the tradeoff visible and the elimination defensible. No schema change in v1 — just the rationale.
